title: Hijack Execution Flow: Dylib Hijacking
summary: Dylib hijacking is the macOS form of library hijacking: a malicious dynamic library (dylib) is placed where an application will look for it at run time. The dynamic loader walks a list of search paths in order, and entries written with the @rpath prefix let an application resolve libraries relative to its own location, which gives an attacker a predictable place to plant a file. Weak linking makes the technique easier, because an application built with an optional library reference such as LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB still starts when that library is absent, so nothing appears broken while the attacker supplies the missing piece. Once loaded, the dylib lives in the application's address space and inherits its privilege level, its file access and its network access. Detection looks at library load records, at files written into application bundles or user library folders, and at code signing status, since an unsigned library inside a signed bundle stands out.

beginner.definition: A dynamic library on macOS is a file of shared code that applications load while they run. This sub-technique means placing a malicious library where an application will find it first. The application then runs the attacker's code as part of itself. It is the macOS branch of the Hijack Execution Flow parent.
beginner.whyItMatters: Applications usually run with the user's permissions and trust. Code loaded inside them looks like the application itself. That can give access to files, the network and sometimes higher privileges. Because a missing optional library does not stop the app, the trick can stay hidden. You need to check which libraries each application really loads.
howItWorks: macOS loads the dynamic libraries that an application lists when it starts.
The loader follows a search path order and takes the first matching file it finds.
Some library paths are relative, written with a prefix that points near the app.
Weak linking means an application still starts even when an expected library is missing.
The attacker places a malicious library with that name in a searched folder.
The library loads into the application and gains its permissions and resources.
beginner.example: Imagine a school library with one shelf for each class. The teacher asks for a book by title and takes the first copy on the shelf. Someone puts a fake copy with the same title at the front. The teacher takes it without checking the cover or the author. Dylib hijacking works like that. The application asks for a library by name and takes the first match. The loaded file is not the one the developer intended.
takeaways: macOS applications search for libraries in a fixed order of paths.
A missing optional library can hide the attack from the user.
Check the signature and location of libraries inside application bundles.

objectives: Define a dylib and describe how macOS loads it at run time.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the Hijack Execution Flow parent.
Describe weak linking and explain why it helps an attacker.
Explain the permissions and resources a loaded library inherits from its host.
Identify evidence such as library load records and application bundle changes.
